title: Reading real Latin
goal: Take apart authentic Latin sentences step by step, read inscriptions and proverbs without a translation, and finish two real, unsimplified readings.
bekal: take apart long sentences with five steps that never change
read twenty authentic Latin sentences and know where they come from
finish two real readings: Caesar's opening and the first three verses of Genesis

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Schola ultima
dialogs.intro: The last lesson. Today Titus hasn't brought a textbook, but sentences that people really wrote.

notes: **Alea iacta est — the perfect passive in two words.** Exactly the pattern you saw in Unit 18: the adjective form *iacta* plus *est*. *Alea* is feminine, so the adjective form is *iacta*, not *iactum*. Suetonius wrote it in the order *iacta alea est*, and according to Plutarch Caesar actually said it in Greek. Caesar is said to have spoken it while crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC, and ever since it has meant "there's no turning back".

**Marcus Spendusam amat — real wall graffiti.** This sentence really was scratched on a wall in Pompeii and can still be read today. You've had everything you need to read it since Unit 3: subject, object ending in *-am*, a group-one verb at the end.

**Verba volant, scripta manent.** Four words, two sentences, not a single conjunction. Latin loves parallel structures like this, and that's what makes its proverbs easy to remember: *verba* against *scripta*, *volant* against *manent*.

**Muri Pompeiorum pleni sunt talibus verbis.** Note that *plenus* is followed by the with/in form. Some Latin adjectives demand a particular form after them: *plenus* (full of), *dignus* (worthy of), *similis* (similar to, with the "of" form). These are things you learn fastest by reading, not from tables.

sections.title: Five steps to take a sentence apart

blocks.text: Real Latin sentences are often long, and their order isn't what you expect. Don't read them left to right as you would English. Use this order, always the same, until it becomes a habit.

items: **One — find the verb.** Usually at the end. Its ending tells you both who the subject is and when it happens. If it ends in *-t*, the subject is one person; if *-nt*, several; if *-tur*, the sentence is passive.
**Two — find the subject.** A noun in the subject form whose number matches the verb. If there isn't one, the subject is already contained in the verb itself.
**Three — find the object.** A word ending in *-m* in the singular, or *-s* in the plural. If there isn't one, the verb may simply not need an object.
**Four — gather the extra details.** Prepositions with their nouns, with/in forms standing alone, time words.

**Five — attach adjectives and clauses where they belong.** An adjective attaches to the noun with exactly the same gender, number, and job; *qui* attaches to the nearest noun that matches its gender and number.

blocks.text: Two of them deserve a second reading. *Non fui, fui, non sum, non curo* uses four verbs you've known since Units 1 and 13 — and it's one of the boldest sentences ever carved in stone. *Vixit annos XXV* shows the object form for length of time, exactly as you learned in Unit 17.

blocks.title: Where you'll find them
items: Many universities still carry Latin mottoes on their crests — *Veritas* (Harvard), *Lux et veritas* (Yale), *Dominus illuminatio mea* (Oxford) — and now you can take them apart yourself.
The scientific names of plants and animals are all Latin: *Homo sapiens* ("wise human"), *Rafflesia arnoldii*, *Oryza sativa* ("cultivated rice").
Legal terms: *in dubio pro reo*, *nemo iudex in causa sua*, *pacta sunt servanda*, *actus reus*.
Medical and pharmacy terms are almost entirely Latin, including prescription abbreviations such as *p.r.n.* (*pro re nata*, "as needed") and *b.i.d.* (*bis in die*, "twice a day").

blocks.text: The two texts below are not simplified at all. Both are among the most famous opening sentences in the history of Latin, and you can now read both.
One — Caesar opens his book (De Bello Gallico I.1)
*Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres, quarum unam incolunt Belgae, aliam Aquitani, tertiam qui ipsorum lingua Celtae, nostra Galli appellantur.*

head: Word
Its form
Meaning
rows: Gaul as a whole is divided

blocks.text: The translation: "Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts; one is inhabited by the Belgae, another by the Aquitani, and the third by those who in their own language are called Celts, in ours Gauls." Note that Caesar writes *nostra* without repeating the word *lingua* — a very Latin habit.
Two — the first three verses of Genesis (Vulgate)
*In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram. Terra autem erat inanis et vacua, et tenebrae super faciem abyssi, et spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas. Dixitque Deus: "Fiat lux." Et facta est lux.*

head: Word
Its form
Meaning
rows: upon the face of the deep

blocks.text: *Fiat lux* uses the only form you've never met: the wish form, which this book deliberately saves for the next level. Apart from those two words, the whole passage is built from material already in your head.

blocks.title: How far you've come
items: You have just read Caesar and the Vulgate without a side-by-side translation. That's no small thing: two thousand years stand between those sentences and this page.
The only thing you don't have yet is one big family of forms — the wish forms and participles. That's what the next level holds, and it builds on everything you've memorized rather than replacing it.
From today, your best way to learn changes: not memorizing new tables, but reading as many easy sentences as you can. Look for illustrated Latin readers for beginners and read every day.
*Macte virtute* — keep going. This language will never change again, and whatever you learn today will still be right a hundred years from now.

exercises.prompt: Translate these authentic sentences into English.
Name the form of the word in brackets: subject, object, of, to, or with/in.

items: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
The children write on the walls.
We read the words of the Romans.
I came, I saw, I conquered.
